title: Chapter 65 — The Whale as a Dish
paragraphs: That a mortal man should dine on the very creature that fuels his lamp, and, like Stubb, eat him by his own light, so to speak, seems so outlandish a thing that we have to look a little into its history and philosophy.

The records show that three centuries ago the Right Whale's tongue was prized as a great delicacy in France, where it fetched high prices. They also show that in the time of Henry VIII a certain court cook won a handsome reward for inventing an admirable sauce to go with barbecued porpoises, which, you will remember, are a species of whale. Porpoises, in fact, are still thought fine eating today. The meat is rolled into balls about the size of billiard balls, and when well seasoned and spiced it could pass for turtle-balls or veal balls. The old monks of Dunfermline loved them. The crown had given them a large grant of porpoises.

The fact is that, among his hunters at least, the whale would be considered a noble dish by all hands, were there not so much of him; but when you come to sit down before a meat-pie nearly one hundred feet long, it takes away your appetite. Only the most unprejudiced of men, like Stubb, eat cooked whale nowadays; but the Eskimos are not so fastidious. We all know how they live on whales, and keep rare old vintages of prime old train oil. Zogranda, one of their most famous doctors, recommends strips of blubber for infants, as being exceedingly juicy and nourishing. And this reminds me of certain Englishmen who long ago were accidentally left behind in Greenland by a whaling vessel: these men actually lived for several months on the moldy scraps of whales that had been left ashore after the blubber was tried out (boiled down for oil). Among the Dutch whalemen these scraps are called "fritters," which, indeed, they greatly resemble, being brown and crisp, and smelling something like old Amsterdam housewives' doughnuts, or oly-cooks, when fresh. They look so edible that the most self-denying stranger can hardly keep his hands off them.

But what further lowers the whale as a civilized dish is his exceeding richness. He is the great prize ox of the sea, too fat to be delicately good. Look at his hump, which would be as fine eating as the buffalo's (which is prized as a rare dish), were it not such a solid pyramid of fat. But the spermaceti itself — how bland and creamy that is, like the transparent, half-jellied white meat of a coconut in the third month of its growth; yet far too rich to serve as a substitute for butter. Nevertheless, many whalemen have a way of absorbing it into some other substance and then eating it. In the long try-watches of the night it is a common thing for the seamen to dip their ship's biscuit into the huge oil-pots and let it fry there a while. I have made many a good supper that way.

With a small Sperm Whale, the brains are considered a fine dish. The casket of the skull is broken into with an axe, and the two plump, whitish lobes are drawn out (looking exactly like two large puddings); they are then mixed with flour and cooked into a most delectable mess, in flavor somewhat like calves' head, which is quite a dish among some epicures; and everyone knows that some young bucks among the epicures, by continually dining on calves' brains, by and by come to have a little brains of their own, enough to tell a calf's head from their own heads — which, indeed, takes uncommon discrimination. And that is why a young buck with an intelligent-looking calf's head before him is somehow one of the saddest sights you can see. The head looks at him in a sort of reproachful way, with an "Et tu, Brute!" expression.

Perhaps it is not entirely because the whale is so extremely oily that landsmen seem to find the idea of eating him abhorrent. That seems to stem, somehow, from the point already made: that a man should eat a freshly murdered creature of the sea, and eat it by its own light at that. But no doubt the first man who ever murdered an ox was regarded as a murderer; perhaps they hanged him; and if oxen had put him on trial, they certainly would have — and he certainly deserved it, if any murderer does. Go to the meat market on a Saturday night and look at the crowds of live bipeds gazing up at the long rows of dead quadrupeds. Doesn't that sight knock a tooth out of the cannibal's jaw? Cannibals? Who isn't a cannibal? I tell you, it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the Fijian who salted a lean missionary down in his cellar to see him through a coming famine — more tolerable for that provident Fijian, I say — than for you, civilized and enlightened gourmand, who nail geese to the ground and feast on their bloated livers in your pâté de foie gras.

But Stubb eats the whale by its own light, does he? And that adds insult to injury, does it? Take a look at your knife handle there, my civilized and enlightened gourmand, as you dine on that roast beef. What is the handle made of? What else but the bones of the brother of the very ox you are eating? And what do you pick your teeth with after polishing off that fat goose? A feather from the same bird. And what quill did the Secretary of the Society for the Suppression of Cruelty to Ganders use to pen his official circulars? Only in the last month or two has that society passed a resolution to use nothing but steel pens.
